Spatial Correction of Field Trial Data

Step-by-step guide to spatial_correct_gam.R

14 March 2026

1 Background: the spatial correction problem

1.1 What is spatial variation?

Greenhouse and field trials rarely provide a perfectly uniform growing environment. Temperature gradients, irrigation patterns, differential light exposure, bench-edge drying, and soil heterogeneity all create structured variation in the measured phenotype that has nothing to do with the genotypes being evaluated. This environmental signal is called spatial variation.

A typical example: pots placed near a greenhouse wall receive less light and experience cooler night temperatures than pots in the centre of the bench. As a result, plants near the wall yield less — not because they are genetically inferior, but because their microenvironment was unfavourable.

1.2 Why does it matter?

When genotypes are assigned to positions at random (as they should be), spatial variation becomes confounded noise: a genotype that happened to be placed in a high-performing zone will appear falsely superior, while one placed in a low-performing zone will appear falsely inferior. The bias in the estimated genotype means — the raw treatment means — can easily exceed the true genetic differences we are trying to detect.

The goal of spatial correction is to separate the genetic signal from the environmental noise, recovering genotype estimates that are free of the spatial trend. The corrected values are called BLUEs (Best Linear Unbiased Estimators) when genotype is modelled as a fixed effect.

1.3 How spatial_correct_gam.R works

The script fits a Generalised Additive Mixed Model (GAMM) using the mgcv package. The spatial surface is captured by a two-dimensional P-spline tensor product smooth (te(Row, Col, bs='ps')), supplemented by row and column random effects (s(row_f, bs='re')) that absorb any remaining directional trends. Genotype is included as a fixed effect with no intercept, so each coefficient is directly the BLUE for that genotype on the phenotype scale.

Single bench: one GAM per bench, one spatial surface per bench.

Multi-bench (this guide): a single joint GAM fitted across all benches simultaneously, with a separate spatial surface per bench (te(..., by = bench_f)) and bench as an additional fixed effect. Fitting all benches jointly borrows strength across benches when estimating genotype effects.

2 Prerequisites

The workflow uses two scripts from this project. Source them before running any analysis.

# Load simulation functions
source("../scripts/simulate_spatial_data.R")

# Load spatial correction functions (guard prevents the script's
# execution block from running when sourced this way)
options(spatial_gam_source_only = TRUE)
source("../scripts/spatial_correct_gam.R")
options(spatial_gam_source_only = NULL)

Functions now available:

Script Functions loaded
simulate_spatial_data.R simulate_field_trial(), plot_bench_heatmap(), plot_all_bench_heatmaps()
spatial_correct_gam.R adaptive_nseg(), read_input(), empirical_semivariogram(), plot_heatmap(), plot_variogram(), make_diagnostic_plots(), fit_mgcv_bench(), fit_mgcv_joint()

3 Step 1: Simulate a trial dataset

3.1 The experimental design

We simulate a multi-bench greenhouse trial with the following structure:

  • 4 benches (Bench1–Bench4)
  • 8 rows × 30 columns per bench → 240 genotypes
  • Each genotype appears once per bench (unreplicated within each bench, but with one observation per bench across 4 benches)
  • Edge-effect spatial pattern (type 6): values elevated at bench borders with a diagonal asymmetry, mimicking common glasshouse conditions
  • Spatial severity increases across benches (intensities 15 → 60) to show how the model handles both mild and severe spatial gradients

The data-generating model is:

\[y_{ij} = g_i + s_j + \varepsilon_{ij}\]

where \(g_i \sim N(55,\ 12^2)\) is the true genotype effect, \(s_j\) is the spatial deviation at plot \(j\) (zero-centred per bench), and \(\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0,\ 4^2)\) is random plot noise.

3.2 Running the simulation

sim <- simulate_field_trial(
  n_bench                     = 4,
  n_rows                      = 8,
  n_cols                      = 30,
  mean_pheno                  = 55,
  sd_geno                     = 12,
  spatial_type                = 6,          # edge effects
  spatial_intensity           = 30,
  spatial_type_per_bench      = rep(6, 4),
  spatial_intensity_per_bench = c(15, 25, 40, 60),
  spatial_scale               = 1,
  sd_error                    = 4,
  pheno_min                   = 0,
  pheno_max                   = 100,
  pheno_name                  = "BNI",
  save_csv                    = TRUE,
  output_dir                  = "data",     # saved to docs/data/
  seed                        = 42
)
## Data written to:          data/BNI_simulation.csv 
## True effects written to:  data/BNI_true_effects.csv
dfr          <- sim$data
true_effects <- sim$true_effects
pheno        <- sim$pheno_name

cat("Rows:", nrow(dfr), "\n")
## Rows: 960
cat("Genotypes:", length(unique(dfr$Genotype)), "\n")
## Genotypes: 240
cat("Benches:", paste(sort(unique(dfr$Bench)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Benches: Bench1, Bench2, Bench3, Bench4

The simulate_field_trial() call writes two files to docs/data/:

  • BNI_simulation.csv — the plot-level dataset you would pass to spatial_correct_gam.R (columns: Bench, Genotype, Row, Col, True_Spatial, BNI)
  • BNI_true_effects.csv — the underlying genotype effects (columns: Genotype, True_BNI); used here to validate the correction but not available in a real experiment

3.3 The raw observed data

benches   <- sort(unique(dfr$Bench))
raw_lims  <- range(dfr[[pheno]], na.rm = TRUE)

raw_plots <- lapply(seq_along(benches), function(i) {
  plot_bench_heatmap(
    bench_dfr     = dfr[dfr$Bench == benches[i], ],
    pheno         = pheno,
    bench_label   = paste0(benches[i], "  (intensity = ",
                           c(15, 25, 40, 60)[i], ")"),
    shared_limits = raw_lims
  )
})

p_raw <- wrap_plots(raw_plots, ncol = 2) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Raw observed BNI values",
    subtitle = "Shared colour scale. Spatial intensity increases Bench1 → Bench4.",
    theme    = theme(plot.title    = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
                     plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey40"))
  )
p_raw

Raw observed BNI values across all four benches. Note how the colour pattern differs from bench to bench despite genotypes being randomly assigned — this is the spatial signal we need to remove. 

ggsave("figures/guide_raw_observed.png", p_raw,
       width = 14, height = 7, dpi = 150)

4 Step 2: Understand the problem

4.1 The hidden spatial pattern

In a real experiment we cannot observe the spatial pattern directly — we only see the phenotype, which confounds genetics and environment. Here, because we simulated the data, we can look at the true spatial contribution at each plot.

sp_lims <- range(dfr$True_Spatial, na.rm = TRUE)

sp_plots <- lapply(seq_along(benches), function(i) {
  plot_bench_heatmap(
    bench_dfr     = dfr[dfr$Bench == benches[i], ],
    pheno         = "True_Spatial",
    bench_label   = paste0(benches[i], "  (intensity = ",
                           c(15, 25, 40, 60)[i], ")"),
    shared_limits = sp_lims
  )
})

p_sp <- wrap_plots(sp_plots, ncol = 2) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "True spatial contributions",
    subtitle = "Edge-effect pattern (type 6). Values are zero-centred per bench.",
    theme    = theme(plot.title    = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
                     plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey40"))
  )
p_sp

True spatial contributions used during simulation. The edge-effect pattern is clear: border plots are elevated, interior plots are depressed. The diagonal asymmetry (top-left high, bottom-right low) is also visible. Intensity increases from Bench1 to Bench4. 

ggsave("figures/guide_true_spatial.png", p_sp,
       width = 14, height = 7, dpi = 150)

4.2 How spatial variation biases estimates

Without spatial correction, the standard approach is to use the raw mean phenotype per genotype. Because genotypes were placed randomly on the bench, a genotype that happened to land in a high-spatial zone will have an inflated mean; one in a low-spatial zone will be deflated.

unc <- aggregate(dfr[[pheno]], list(Genotype = dfr$Genotype), mean)
colnames(unc)[2] <- "Mean"
unc_m <- merge(unc, true_effects, by = "Genotype")

r_unc    <- round(cor(unc_m$Mean,  unc_m$True_BNI), 4)
rmse_unc <- round(sqrt(mean((unc_m$Mean - unc_m$True_BNI)^2)), 2)

ggplot(unc_m, aes(x = True_BNI, y = Mean)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5, colour = "#e55c00") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey30",
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Uncorrected means vs true genotype effects",
    subtitle = paste0("r = ", r_unc, "   RMSE = ", rmse_unc),
    x        = "True BNI",
    y        = "Uncorrected mean BNI"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40"))

Uncorrected genotype means (averaged across benches) versus true genotype effects. The scatter around the 1:1 line reveals the bias introduced by spatial variation. The RMSE and correlation quantify how well raw means recover the truth. 

cat(sprintf("Uncorrected means:  r = %.4f,  RMSE = %.2f\n", r_unc, rmse_unc))
## Uncorrected means:  r = 0.9472,  RMSE = 4.07

The RMSE and correlation will improve substantially after spatial correction.

5 Step 3: Configure spatial_correct_gam.R

5.1 The configuration block

Open scripts/spatial_correct_gam.R in your editor. The only section you need to modify is the USER CONFIGURATION block at the very top of the file:

# ── USER CONFIGURATION ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
data_file      <- "data/mydata.csv"   # path to your CSV or .rda file
output_dir     <- "output/gam"        # where to write results

# Column names in your data
pheno_cols     <- c("yield")          # one or more trait columns
geno_col       <- "Genotype"          # genotype identifier
row_col        <- "Row"               # row coordinate (numeric)
col_col        <- "Column"            # column coordinate (numeric)
bench_col      <- NULL                # bench/trial column (NULL = single bench)

# Model options
estimate_type  <- "BLUEs"            # "BLUEs", "BLUPs", or "both"
k_row          <- NULL               # NULL = auto; or integer basis dim for rows
k_col          <- NULL               # NULL = auto; or integer basis dim for cols
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For our simulated dataset the settings are:

# Mirror the config block you would edit in the script
data_file     <- "data/BNI_simulation.csv"
output_dir    <- "data/gam_output"

pheno_cols    <- c("BNI")
geno_col      <- "Genotype"
row_col       <- "Row"
col_col       <- "Col"
bench_col     <- "Bench"      # multi-bench design

estimate_type <- "BLUEs"
k_row         <- NULL         # auto
k_col         <- NULL         # auto

5.1.1 Key configuration decisions

Setting What to set Notes
data_file Path to your CSV or .rda Auto-detected by extension
pheno_cols All trait columns you want to correct Can be a vector, e.g. c("yield", "height")
geno_col Genotype/variety identifier Must be character or convertible to factor
row_col / col_col Numeric row/column coordinates Must be numeric; no NAs allowed
bench_col Bench/trial identifier, or NULL NULL triggers single-bench model; column present triggers joint multi-bench model
estimate_type "BLUEs" (default), "BLUPs", or "both" BLUEs treat genotype as fixed (unbiased, no shrinkage). BLUPs treat genotype as random (shrinkage toward mean — use when genotypes are a sample of a larger population)
k_row / k_col NULL for auto, or an integer Basis dimension for the spatial smoother. Auto rule: min(max(5, floor(n_unique/2)), 20). Increase for very large grids

6 Step 4: Run the spatial correction

6.1 Load and validate the data

The script checks all required columns, verifies coordinate columns are numeric, and warns if the grid is too small for the spatial smoother to be identifiable.

# Read the simulated CSV
data <- read_input(data_file)

cat("── Data summary ───────────────────────────────────────────\n")
## ── Data summary ───────────────────────────────────────────
cat("  Rows:", nrow(data), "\n")
##   Rows: 960
cat("  Genotypes:", length(unique(data[[geno_col]])), "\n")
##   Genotypes: 240
cat("  Benches:", paste(sort(unique(data[[bench_col]])), collapse = ", "), "\n")
##   Benches: Bench1, Bench2, Bench3, Bench4
cat("  Grid (rows × cols):",
    length(unique(data[[row_col]])), "×",
    length(unique(data[[col_col]])), "\n")
##   Grid (rows × cols): 8 × 30
cat("  Traits:", paste(pheno_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
##   Traits: BNI

6.2 Fit the joint multi-bench model

Because bench_col is set, the script automatically uses fit_mgcv_joint(), which fits a single GAM across all four benches simultaneously.

The model formula built internally is:

BNI ~ 0 + Genotype + bench_f +
      te(Row, Col, bs=c('ps','ps'), k=c(kr,kc), by=bench_f) +
      s(row_f, bench_f, bs='re') +
      s(col_f, bench_f, bs='re')

where:

  • 0 + Genotype — no intercept; each coefficient is directly a BLUE
  • bench_f — bench fixed effect (accounts for mean-level differences between benches)
  • te(..., by=bench_f) — a separate 2D P-spline spatial surface for each bench; smoothness estimated via REML
  • s(row_f, bench_f, bs='re') and s(col_f, bench_f, bs='re') — row and column random effects nested within bench; absorb residual directional trends
if (!dir.exists(output_dir)) dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE)

result <- fit_mgcv_joint(
  data      = data,
  pheno     = "BNI",
  geno_col  = geno_col,
  row_col   = row_col,
  col_col   = col_col,
  bench_col = bench_col
)

cat("Model converged:", result$converged, "\n")
## Model converged: TRUE
cat("Spatial EDF:", round(result$edf_spatial, 1), "\n")
## Spatial EDF: 67.7
cat("Residual SD:", round(sd(result$residuals, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
## Residual SD: 3.43
cat("BLUEs extracted for", nrow(result$blues), "genotypes\n")
## BLUEs extracted for 240 genotypes

The effective degrees of freedom (EDF) of the spatial smoother is a useful diagnostic. A large EDF (e.g. > 10) indicates the model needed a complex surface to capture the spatial pattern — expected here given the edge-effect structure. An EDF close to 1 would suggest the spatial pattern is nearly linear.

7 Step 5: Understand the output files

When you run spatial_correct_gam.R as a standalone script (with Rscript), it writes all outputs to output_dir. Here we write them manually to docs/data/gam_output/ to keep the guide self-contained.

7.1 BLUEs.csv

One row per genotype, one column per trait (plus a standard error column). These are the primary output — the spatially corrected genotype estimates you would carry forward into downstream analyses.

blues_df <- result$blues
names(blues_df)[names(blues_df) == "BLUE"]    <- "BNI"
names(blues_df)[names(blues_df) == "BLUE_SE"] <- "BNI_SE"

write.csv(blues_df, file.path(output_dir, "BLUEs.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

cat("── BLUEs.csv ──────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
## ── BLUEs.csv ──────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("  Rows:", nrow(blues_df), "\n")
##   Rows: 240
cat("  Columns:", paste(names(blues_df), collapse = ", "), "\n\n")
##   Columns: Genotype, BNI, BNI_SE
head(blues_df, 8)
##   Genotype      BNI   BNI_SE
## 1     G001 70.56270 2.204190
## 2     G002 46.36817 2.196896
## 3     G003 61.45541 2.261945
## 4     G004 59.92914 2.305650
## 5     G005 58.02352 2.246965
## 6     G006 50.10817 2.210991
## 7     G007 74.73500 2.237141
## 8     G008 55.12412 2.195711

The BNI_SE column is the standard error of the BLUE, derived from the diagonal of the model’s variance–covariance matrix. It reflects uncertainty in the genotype estimate due to the random noise in the data; it does not include uncertainty in the spatial surface itself.

7.2 spatial_trends.csv

One row per plot, with the estimated spatial contribution at each position. This is useful for quality control and for understanding where spatial correction was large.

sp_df <- data[, c(geno_col, row_col, col_col, bench_col), drop = FALSE]
sp_df$spatial_trend <- result$spatial

write.csv(sp_df, file.path(output_dir, "spatial_trends.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

cat("── spatial_trends.csv ─────────────────────────────────────\n")
## ── spatial_trends.csv ─────────────────────────────────────
cat("  Rows:", nrow(sp_df), "\n")
##   Rows: 960
cat("  Spatial range: [",
    round(min(sp_df$spatial_trend), 2), ",",
    round(max(sp_df$spatial_trend), 2), "]\n")
##   Spatial range: [ -22.56 , 22.54 ]

7.3 model_summary.csv

Per-trait (and per-bench, for multi-bench models) fit statistics.

sum_df <- data.frame(
  pheno       = "BNI",
  bench       = "joint",
  resid_sd    = round(sd(result$residuals, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
  edf_spatial = round(result$edf_spatial, 2),
  converged   = result$converged
)

write.csv(sum_df, file.path(output_dir, "model_summary.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(sum_df)
##   pheno bench resid_sd edf_spatial converged
## 1   BNI joint     3.43       67.67      TRUE
Column Meaning
resid_sd Residual standard deviation after spatial correction. Smaller = better fit
edf_spatial Effective degrees of freedom consumed by the spatial smooth(s). Reflects complexity of the estimated surface
converged Whether the REML optimisation converged. A FALSE here warrants investigation

8 Step 6: Interpret the diagnostic plots

The make_diagnostic_plots() function produces a 6-panel diagnostic figure for each bench. These plots are the key tool for checking whether the spatial correction worked correctly.

for (b in benches) {
  b_mask  <- data[[bench_col]] == b
  b_data  <- data[b_mask, ]
  b_res   <- list(
    spatial   = result$spatial[b_mask],
    residuals = result$residuals[b_mask],
    fitted    = result$fitted[b_mask]
  )

  p_diag <- make_diagnostic_plots(b_data, b_res, pheno = "BNI",
                                   row_col = row_col, col_col = col_col,
                                   bench_label = b)

  ggsave(
    file.path("figures", paste0("guide_diagnostics_BNI_", b, ".png")),
    p_diag, width = 14, height = 9, dpi = 150
  )
}

# Display Bench4 (most instructive — highest spatial intensity)
b        <- "Bench4"
b_mask   <- data[[bench_col]] == b
b_data   <- data[b_mask, ]
b_res    <- list(
  spatial   = result$spatial[b_mask],
  residuals = result$residuals[b_mask],
  fitted    = result$fitted[b_mask]
)
make_diagnostic_plots(b_data, b_res, pheno = "BNI",
                      row_col = row_col, col_col = col_col,
                      bench_label = "Bench4 (intensity = 60)")

Six-panel diagnostic for Bench4 (highest spatial intensity). Top row: what the model sees. Bottom row: how well it absorbed the spatial signal.

8.1 Panel-by-panel interpretation

8.1.1 Panel 1 — Observed heatmap (top-left)

Shows the raw measured values at each plot position, exactly as recorded. The spatial pattern is visible as structured colour gradients: if border plots are consistently darker or lighter than interior plots, there is a spatial signal.

What to look for: any systematic colour pattern (gradient, edge effect, striping). Random salt-and-pepper colour is measurement noise and is expected.

8.1.2 Panel 2 — Spatial trend heatmap (top-centre)

The estimated spatial surface from the te() smoother — what the model attributes to the physical location rather than the genotype. This is the “environmental landscape” the model has learned.

What to look for: the surface should look like a smooth, plausible environmental gradient. If it shows the same spatial structure as the observed data (Panel 1), the model is capturing the signal. If it is flat or noisy, the spatial smoother may be under-fitted (try larger k_row/k_col).

8.1.3 Panel 3 — Residuals heatmap (top-right)

The corrected residuals: observed values minus the full model fit (genotype effect + spatial surface + random effects). These represent what remains unexplained.

What to look for: the residuals should show no systematic spatial structure — they should look like random noise. If you can still see a gradient or edge effect in the residuals, the spatial correction was incomplete (the smoother may not have had enough flexibility). Compare the colour scale range in Panel 3 to Panel 1: a large reduction indicates effective correction.

8.1.4 Panel 4 — Variogram of observed values (bottom-left)

An empirical semivariogram of the raw observed phenotype. The semivariance \(\hat{\gamma}(h) = \frac{1}{2} \text{E}[(y_i - y_j)^2]\) is plotted against the distance \(h\) between plot pairs.

What to look for: a rising variogram indicates spatial autocorrelation — nearby plots are more similar than distant plots. The rise should be steep when spatial gradients are strong. A flat variogram would mean no spatial structure.

8.1.5 Panel 5 — Variogram of corrected residuals (bottom-centre)

The same semivariogram computed on the corrected residuals instead of the raw values. After successful spatial correction the variogram should be flat (approximately constant semivariance across all distances), indicating that the residuals are spatially uncorrelated.

What to look for: the sill (plateau level) should be much lower than in Panel 4, and the variogram should be approximately flat from small distances onwards. A rising corrected variogram means spatial autocorrelation remains in the residuals — the correction was insufficient.

8.1.6 Panel 6 — QQ plot of corrected residuals (bottom-right)

A quantile–quantile plot comparing the distribution of corrected residuals to a theoretical normal distribution. Points falling on the diagonal line are consistent with normality.

What to look for: the central range of the residuals should track the diagonal closely. Systematic deviations at the tails (heavy tails or asymmetry) may indicate outliers, non-normality of the error distribution, or genotypes with an unusually large true effect that the model is struggling with.

9 Step 7: Check all four benches

Compare the diagnostic plots across benches to see how increasing spatial intensity affects the correction.

data$spatial_est <- result$spatial
sp_est_lims <- range(data$spatial_est, na.rm = TRUE)

sp_est_plots <- lapply(seq_along(benches), function(i) {
  plot_bench_heatmap(
    bench_dfr     = data[data$Bench == benches[i], ],
    pheno         = "spatial_est",
    bench_label   = paste0(benches[i], "  (intensity = ",
                           c(15, 25, 40, 60)[i], ")"),
    shared_limits = sp_est_lims
  )
})

p_sp_est <- wrap_plots(sp_est_plots, ncol = 2) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Estimated spatial trends (joint model)",
    subtitle = "Shared colour scale. Compare to true spatial patterns above.",
    theme    = theme(plot.title    = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
                     plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey40"))
  )
p_sp_est

Estimated spatial trend surfaces for all four benches on a shared colour scale. The model captures both the edge-effect structure and the increasing intensity from Bench1 to Bench4. 

ggsave("figures/guide_estimated_spatial.png", p_sp_est,
       width = 14, height = 7, dpi = 150)

10 Step 8: Validate the correction

Because this is simulated data, we can compare the recovered BLUEs directly to the true genotype effects to quantify how well the correction worked.

merged <- merge(blues_df[, c(geno_col, "BNI")], true_effects, by = "Genotype")

r_blue    <- round(cor(merged$BNI, merged$True_BNI), 4)
rmse_blue <- round(sqrt(mean((merged$BNI - merged$True_BNI)^2)), 2)

ggplot(merged, aes(x = True_BNI, y = BNI)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5, colour = "#2c7bb6") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey30",
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Corrected BLUEs vs true genotype effects",
    subtitle = paste0("r = ", r_blue, "   RMSE = ", rmse_blue),
    x        = "True BNI",
    y        = "BLUE (mgcv joint)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40"))

Spatially corrected BLUEs (joint mgcv model) versus true genotype effects. Compare to the uncorrected means plot above: the cloud is tighter around the 1:1 line, RMSE is smaller, and correlation is higher. 

cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
## ─────────────────────────────────────────────
cat(sprintf("  %-25s  r = %.4f   RMSE = %.2f\n",
            "Uncorrected means:", r_unc, rmse_unc))
##   Uncorrected means:         r = 0.9472   RMSE = 4.07
cat(sprintf("  %-25s  r = %.4f   RMSE = %.2f\n",
            "Joint mgcv BLUEs:", r_blue, rmse_blue))
##   Joint mgcv BLUEs:          r = 0.9832   RMSE = 2.19
cat("─────────────────────────────────────────────\n")
## ─────────────────────────────────────────────

The reduction in RMSE and increase in correlation demonstrate that the spatial correction successfully recovered genotype effects that are much closer to the truth than the raw means.

11 Step 9: Extras — BLUE distribution and spatial surfaces

The standalone script also saves two summary plots automatically. We reproduce them here.

11.1 BLUE distribution

ggplot(blues_df, aes(x = BNI)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 35, fill = "#2c7bb6", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_density(colour = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of BLUEs: BNI",
       x = "BLUE value", y = "Density") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))

Distribution of BLUEs. A roughly normal shape centred on the grand mean is expected when genotype effects are drawn from a normal distribution. Unusual spikes or heavy tails may indicate a few genotypes with very extreme values.

11.2 Spatial surfaces (shared scale)

p_sp_est

Estimated spatial trend surfaces for all four benches. These are saved to spatial_surfaces.png in the output directory by the standalone script.

12 Running the standalone script

Once you understand the workflow, normal use is simply:

1. Edit the configuration block at the top of scripts/spatial_correct_gam.R to match your data file and column names.

2. Run the script from the terminal:

Rscript scripts/spatial_correct_gam.R

Or from an R session:

source("scripts/spatial_correct_gam.R")

The script will print a summary as it runs and write all outputs to output_dir.

What gets created:

File Description
BLUEs.csv One row per genotype; one value + SE column per trait
BLUPs.csv Same structure, for BLUPs (only if estimate_type = "BLUPs" or "both")
spatial_trends.csv Per-plot estimated spatial effect for quality control
model_summary.csv Residual SD, spatial EDF, convergence status per trait
diagnostics_{trait}_{bench}.png 6-panel diagnostic per bench per trait
blues_distribution.png Histogram + density of BLUEs per trait
spatial_surfaces.png Spatial trend panels for all benches

13 Function reference

13.1 adaptive_nseg(n_unique)

Chooses the number of B-spline basis functions for the spatial smoother automatically from the number of unique positions along one axis.

Rule: min(max(5, floor(n_unique / 2)), 20) — roughly half the unique positions, bounded between 5 and 20. This prevents over-fitting in small grids and under-fitting in large ones.

Argument Type Description
n_unique integer Number of unique positions along one coordinate axis

Returns: integer.

13.2 read_input(fn, rda_object = NULL)

Reads a field trial data file into a data frame.

Supports CSV (.csv) and R binary files (.rda, .RData). For R binary files, the first data frame in the file is returned unless rda_object specifies the object name.

Argument Default Description
fn — Path to the data file
rda_object NULL Name of the object to extract from a .rda file; NULL = use the first data frame found

Returns: data.frame. Stops with an informative message if the file is not found or the extension is not recognised.

13.3 empirical_semivariogram(data, row_col, col_col, value_col, n_bins = 15)

Computes an empirical semivariogram by binning all pairwise plot distances into n_bins lag classes and averaging the squared differences within each class. Only pairs within 60 % of the maximum pairwise distance are included to avoid noisy estimates at long lags.

Argument Default Description
data — data.frame containing the coordinates and value columns
row_col — Name of the row coordinate column
col_col — Name of the column coordinate column
value_col — Name of the value column
n_bins 15 Number of distance lag bins

Returns: data.frame with columns dist (mean distance in each bin) and sv (mean semivariance), sorted by dist. Returns NULL when fewer than 10 non-missing observations are available.

13.4 plot_heatmap(data, row_col, col_col, value_col, title = "", limits = NULL)

Plots a field layout as a colour tile grid using ggplot2. Row 1 is placed at the top (y-axis reversed to match field convention); column 1 is at the left.

Argument Default Description
data — data.frame with coordinates and fill column
row_col — Name of the row coordinate column
col_col — Name of the column coordinate column
value_col — Name of the fill column
title "" Plot title
limits NULL c(min, max) for the viridis fill scale; NULL = auto from data

Returns: ggplot object. Compose multiple plots with patchwork::wrap_plots().

13.5 plot_variogram(vgram, title = "")

Plots an empirical semivariogram returned by empirical_semivariogram(). Returns a blank placeholder panel labelled “Insufficient data” when vgram is NULL or empty, so it is safe to use even when data are sparse.

Argument Default Description
vgram — data.frame with columns dist and sv, as returned by empirical_semivariogram()
title "" Plot title

Returns: ggplot object.

13.6 make_diagnostic_plots(bench_data, result, pheno, row_col, col_col, bench_label = "")

Composes the 6-panel diagnostic figure for one bench × trait combination. Panels (left to right, top to bottom):

  1. Observed — raw phenotype heatmap
  2. Spatial trend — estimated spatial surface from the te() smoother
  3. Residuals — corrected residuals heatmap
  4. Variogram: observed — semivariogram of the raw phenotype
  5. Variogram: residuals — semivariogram of the corrected residuals
  6. QQ plot — quantile–quantile plot of corrected residuals vs. normal
Argument Default Description
bench_data — data.frame for the bench, containing the observed phenotype column
result — Named list with elements $spatial, $residuals, $fitted — as returned by fit_mgcv_bench() or fit_mgcv_joint()
pheno — Name of the phenotype column in bench_data
row_col — Name of the row coordinate column
col_col — Name of the column coordinate column
bench_label "" Label shown in the figure title

Returns: patchwork ggplot (2 × 3 grid). Save with ggsave().

13.7 fit_mgcv_bench(bench_data, pheno, geno_col, row_col, col_col, k_row = NULL, k_col = NULL, estimate_type = "BLUEs")

Fits the te_ps_re spatial correction model for a single bench.

The GAM formula for BLUEs is:

pheno ~ 0 + Genotype + te(Row, Col, bs=c('ps','ps'), k=c(kr,kc)) +
        s(row_f, bs='re') + s(col_f, bs='re')
Argument Default Description
bench_data — data.frame for one bench
pheno — Name of the phenotype column
geno_col — Name of the genotype column
row_col — Name of the row coordinate column
col_col — Name of the column coordinate column
k_row NULL Basis dimension for rows; NULL = determined by adaptive_nseg()
k_col NULL Basis dimension for columns; NULL = determined by adaptive_nseg()
estimate_type "BLUEs" "BLUEs", "BLUPs", or "both"

Returns: named list:

Element Description
$blues data.frame(Genotype, BLUE, BLUE_SE) — NULL if not requested
$blups data.frame(Genotype, BLUP, BLUP_SE) — NULL if not requested
$fitted Numeric vector of model fitted values (length = nrow(bench_data))
$residuals Numeric vector of model residuals
$spatial Numeric vector of estimated spatial contribution at each plot
$converged Logical; whether REML optimisation converged
$edf_spatial Numeric; sum of EDF of all te() smooth terms

13.8 fit_mgcv_joint(data, pheno, geno_col, row_col, col_col, bench_col, k_row = NULL, k_col = NULL, estimate_type = "BLUEs")

Fits the te_ps_re spatial correction model jointly across all benches.

The GAM formula is:

pheno ~ 0 + Genotype + bench_f +
        te(Row, Col, bs=c('ps','ps'), k=c(kr,kc), by=bench_f) +
        s(row_f, bench_f, bs='re') +
        s(col_f, bench_f, bs='re')

The by = bench_f term creates an independent spatial surface for each bench within the single joint model. The basis dimension k is chosen from the minimum bench grid dimension across all benches, ensuring a valid model even when benches differ in size.

Argument Default Description
data — Full data.frame (all benches combined)
pheno — Name of the phenotype column
geno_col — Name of the genotype column
row_col — Name of the row coordinate column
col_col — Name of the column coordinate column
bench_col — Name of the bench identifier column
k_row NULL Basis dimension for rows; NULL = auto
k_col NULL Basis dimension for columns; NULL = auto
estimate_type "BLUEs" Only "BLUEs" is supported for the joint model

Returns: named list with the same structure as fit_mgcv_bench(), except $blues is always populated (joint model only supports BLUEs) and $spatial is the concatenated spatial trend across all benches in the same row order as the input data.
